title: The West Sikkim monastery circuit: Pemayangtse to Tashiding
summary: West Sikkim holds the oldest cluster of Buddhist sites in the state: Dubdi, Sangachoeling, Pemayangtse, Tashiding and the Rabdentse ruins, linked by Yuksom and Khecheopalri Lake. Three days from a Pelling base covers them at an easy pace, with Ralang and Rinchenpong as add-ons.
meta_description: West Sikkim monastery circuit: Pemayangtse, Sangachoeling, Dubdi, Tashiding, Rabdentse, Khecheopalri, Rinchenpong and Ralang. Route, timings, etiquette.

sections.heading: Why these monasteries matter
paras: Buddhism in Sikkim is traced to Guru Padmasambhava, who is said to have blessed the land in the eighth century and hidden sacred teachings in its hills. The organised Buddhist kingdom, though, began in 1642, when three Tibetan lamas of the Nyingma school met at Yuksom and crowned Phuntsog Namgyal as the first Chogyal. In the decades that followed, the lamas and the early kings built the first monasteries of the kingdom on the ridges of what is now West Sikkim.

That is why the oldest and most important Nyingma sites are clustered here, within a day's drive of each other: Dubdi above Yuksom, Sangachoeling and Pemayangtse above Pelling, and Tashiding on its hill between two rivers. The ruins of Rabdentse, the royal capital from 1670, sit among them, and the sacred lakes of Khecheopalri and Kathok belong to the same landscape.

Local tradition describes this area as part of a sacred land laid out by Guru Rinpoche, with Tashiding at its heart. You do not need to be a Buddhist to feel that these places were chosen with care. Each looks out over a wide valley, usually towards Kangchenjunga, which is itself revered as Sikkim's guardian deity.

sections.heading: A three-day route from Pelling
paras: Day one stays close to Pelling. Start at Pemayangtse for the morning prayers and the carved wooden model of Zangdok Palri, Guru Rinpoche's heavenly palace, on the top floor. Walk the forest path to Rabdentse, then spend the afternoon on the ridge above town at Sangachoeling, one of the oldest monasteries in Sikkim, which you can reach by a steep path from Upper Pelling or by road via the Chenrezig statue.

Day two goes north. Drive to Khecheopalri Lake, walk to the prayer-flag jetty, and visit the small monastery above the lake. Continue to Yuksom for the Norbugang coronation throne and Kathok Lake. Fit visitors can climb to Dubdi Monastery in under an hour; others can spend the time in the village. Stay the night in Yuksom if you can, rather than driving back.

Day three crosses to Tashiding, about 19 km from Yuksom. Climb the steep path to the monastery and walk among its chortens and carved mani stones. From Tashiding, continue south to Legship and either return to Pelling, go on to Rinchenpong for its rare Adi Buddha statue, or head east to Ravangla for Ralang Monastery and the Buddha Park.

sections.heading: Etiquette inside monasteries
paras: Sikkim's monasteries are living places of worship, not museums, and the monks are generally welcoming to respectful visitors. A few simple habits go a long way.

Walk clockwise around monasteries, chortens, prayer wheels and mani walls, keeping them on your right. Turn prayer wheels clockwise too. Remove your shoes and hat before entering a prayer hall when asked, and sit with your feet tucked under you or to the side, never pointing at the altar or at monks. Speak quietly, and if prayers are under way, enter only if invited and sit near the door.

Photography rules differ from place to place. Many halls, including the top floor at Pemayangtse, ban photos inside. Always ask first, never use flash near wall paintings, and do not photograph monks during prayers without permission. A small offering in the donation box is welcome but never required.

sections.heading: Festivals worth timing a trip for
paras: The best time to see these monasteries alive is during their festivals. Bumchu at Tashiding, on the 14th and 15th days of the first Tibetan month in February or March, is the most important. Lamas open a sacred vase of water and read its level as a forecast for the year, and pilgrims come from across the Himalaya.

Pemayangtse holds masked cham dances around Losar, the Tibetan New Year, usually in February or March. Ralang's Kagyed dance is held in December, at the end of the Tibetan year. Pang Lhabsol, which honours Kangchenjunga, is marked at Ravangla and Ralang in late August or September. Dates follow the Tibetan lunar calendar and change every year, so check current status before you travel and book rooms early.
Festival days are crowded, noisy and joyful. Arrive early for a spot, dress warmly for the long hours in the courtyard, and keep well clear of the dancers' ground.

sections.heading: Getting around and costs
paras: The circuit is easiest with a reserved car from Pelling, which local drivers know well. Indicative 2025–26 rates are about ₹2,000–2,800 for a half-day loop around Pelling, ₹3,500–4,500 for a full day to Khecheopalri and Yuksom, and ₹3,000–3,500 for a day trip to Tashiding. A three-day circuit with a night in Yuksom, ending in Rinchenpong or Ravangla, usually costs about ₹9,000–12,000 for the car.

Budget travellers can do much of it by shared jeep from Gyalshing, which has morning services to Yuksom, Tashiding and Legship, but connections are thin after midday and you will spend time waiting. Entry fees are low: around ₹20–50 at Pemayangtse, a small Archaeological Survey of India fee at Rabdentse and token or no fees elsewhere.
Hiring a local guide for a day, about ₹1,000–1,500, makes a real difference at Pemayangtse and Tashiding, where much of the meaning lies in the paintings, statues and stories that are not labelled.

sections.heading: Practical tips
paras: Monasteries are at their best in the early morning, when prayers are under way and the light is soft. Many close their main halls at midday and in the late afternoon. Smaller monasteries such as Dubdi and Resum may be locked; ask locally for the caretaker and be patient.

Carry cash for donations, entry fees and tea, as card machines are rare outside Pelling. Wear shoes that slip on and off easily, and socks for cold floors. Bring a light jacket even in summer, as halls are cold inside. In the monsoon, from June to September, paths to Dubdi, Tashiding and Sangachoeling are slippery and leeches are out, so wear proper shoes and carry salt.

faqs.q: Which is the most important monastery in West Sikkim
faqs.a: Pemayangtse and Tashiding are usually counted as the most important. Pemayangtse, founded in 1705, was the premier monastery of the Nyingma order in Sikkim and closely linked to the royal family. Tashiding is regarded as the most sacred site, at the heart of the land blessed by Guru Rinpoche, and hosts Bumchu every spring.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for the monastery circuit
faqs.a: Three days from a Pelling base covers the main sites at an easy pace: Pemayangtse, Rabdentse and Sangachoeling on day one; Khecheopalri Lake and Yuksom on day two; Tashiding on day three. Add a day for Rinchenpong or Ravangla and Ralang. Two days is possible with an early start and less walking.

faqs.q: Is Dubdi the oldest monastery in Sikkim
faqs.a: Dubdi, founded in 1701, is often called the first monastery of the Namgyal kingdom. Sangachoeling, dated to around 1697, and Tashiding, founded in the seventeenth century, also have strong claims, and older shrines and caves existed before. Sources differ, so it is safest to call Dubdi one of the oldest.

faqs.q: Can women visit all the monasteries
faqs.a: Yes. Women can visit all the monasteries on this circuit. Pemayangtse traditionally admitted only male monks of particular lineage, while Sangachoeling has traditionally admitted nuns as well. Some inner shrines, such as protector-deity rooms, may be closed to visitors of any gender. Follow posted signs and the monks' guidance.

faqs.q: Can I take photos inside the monasteries
faqs.a: It depends on the monastery. Many prayer halls, including the top floor of Pemayangtse, do not allow photography. Courtyards and exteriors are usually fine. Always ask a monk first, never use flash near wall paintings, and avoid photographing people at prayer. Respect a refusal without argument.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for the monastery circuit
faqs.a: You do not need one to visit, but a local guide for a day, about ₹1,000–1,500, makes the visits far richer. Few paintings or statues are labelled, and a guide can explain the deities, the history of the Namgyal kings and the meaning of rituals. Ask your hotel in Pelling to arrange one.

faqs.q: What is the best time of year for the circuit
faqs.a: October to December and February to April have dry paths and clear views. February or March brings Bumchu at Tashiding and Losar dances at Pemayangtse, and December brings the Kagyed dance at Ralang. The monsoon months, June to September, make the walks to Dubdi and Tashiding slippery and leech-prone.

faqs.q: Are there entry fees at the monasteries
faqs.a: Fees are low. Pemayangtse charges around ₹20–50, Rabdentse has a small Archaeological Survey of India fee, and most other monasteries are free or ask for a donation. Fees can change, so check current status before you travel. Carry small notes for donation boxes and butter lamp offerings.

faqs.q: Can I do the circuit by public transport
faqs.a: Partly. Shared jeeps run from Gyalshing to Yuksom, Tashiding and Legship, mostly in the morning, and you can walk to Pemayangtse and Sangachoeling from Pelling. Connections are thin after midday, so allow extra time and stay overnight in Yuksom or Tashiding. A reserved car is far easier for a short trip.
